displayQuote: No man will make a great leader who wants to do it all himself, or get all the credit for doing it

meta.title: Who really said "No man will make a great leader who wants to do it all himself, or get all the credit for doing it"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Carnegie really said it — but he said “a great business,” not “a great leader.” The swap is traced to a 1975 newspaper.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'No man will make a great leader who wants to do it all himself, or get all the credit for doing it'?
meta.ogDescription: Andrew Carnegie said it in an 1899 interview — about building a great business, not a great leader. Here's where the word changed.

answer.label: Misquoted — Carnegie said “a great business”
answer.sourceLine: The thought is genuinely Carnegie’s, but one word is wrong: in an interview published 15 October 1899 he said no man will make a great business that way — not a great leader. Quote Investigator ↗ traces the “leader” swap to a Salt Lake City newspaper in 1975, seventy-six years later.

source.heading: Where the real sentence lives

docMeta.dd: Andrew Carnegie: The Man and His Work
Barnard Alderson — Doubleday, Page & Company, New York, 1902; pages 57–58
Interview published 15 October 1899, St. Louis Globe-Democrat, “Carnegie On How To Get Rich”

source.excerpt: I do not believe any one man can make a success of a business nowadays. I am sure I never could have done so without my partners, of whom I had thirty-two, the brightest and cleverest young fellows in the world. All are equal to each other, as the members of the Cabinet are equal. The chief must only be first among equals… The way they differed from me and beat me many a time was delightful to behold. I never enjoyed anything more than to get a sound thrashing in an argument at the hands of these young geniuses. No man will make a great business who wants to do it all himself or to get all the credit for doing it. I believe firmly in youths as executive agents. Older heads should be reserved for counsel.
trail: 15 October 1899 — a syndicated interview, “Carnegie On How To Get Rich,” runs in the St. Louis Globe-Democrat and, the same day, in The Philadelphia Times. It contains the sentence in its original form, with “business” and “credit of doing it,” per Quote Investigator ↗.
1902 — Barnard Alderson’s biography reprints the passage on pages 57–58 with “credit for doing it,” the phrasing the modern quote inherited. Confirmed in the scanned first edition ↗.

15 November 1975 — a Salt Lake City Deseret News item swaps business for leader. It is the earliest “leader” printing in Quote Investigator’s chronology ↗, and a 1997 quotation anthology fixes it under the heading Leadership.

Today — Goodreads ↗ and comparable sites carry the “great leader” wording under Carnegie’s name with no book, date or page — which is why almost nobody quoting it knows he was talking about a company.
source.excerptNote: As printed in Alderson’s 1902 biography, pages 57–58. The 1899 newspaper text of the same interview reads “all the credit of doing it”; Alderson’s “for” is the form the modern quotation inherited.

author.name: Andrew Carnegie
author.heading: Who was Andrew Carnegie?
author.bio: Carnegie emigrated from Dunfermline to Allegheny, Pennsylvania in 1848 at the age of twelve and built the Carnegie Steel Company into the dominant American steel producer, selling it to J. P. Morgan in 1901 in the deal that formed U.S. Steel. He credited that success less to his own effort than to the thirty-two partners he promoted from inside the works — “the brightest and cleverest young fellows in the world.” He spent the rest of his life giving the proceeds away, chiefly to public libraries.

cite.sourceCitation: Barnard Alderson, Andrew Carnegie: The Man and His Work (New York: Doubleday, Page & Company, 1902), 57–58. Carnegie’s remarks were first published in an interview in the St. Louis Globe-Democrat, 15 October 1899, per Quote Investigator.
cite.pageCitation: Quotle.info. “Who really said ‘No man will make a great leader who wants to do it all himself, or get all the credit for doing it’?” Last verified 17 Aug 2026.

copyAttribution: "No man will make a great business who wants to do it all himself or to get all the credit for doing it." —Andrew Carnegie, quoted in Barnard Alderson, Andrew Carnegie: The Man and His Work (New York: Doubleday, Page & Company, 1902), 57–58; from an interview published in the St. Louis Globe-Democrat, 15 October 1899. The familiar "great leader" wording is a later alteration — Carnegie said "business."

misattribution.heading: Right man, wrong word
misattribution.intro: This is not a fabricated quote, and Carnegie is not the wrong name on it. It is something subtler and more common: a real sentence from a real interview that has drifted one noun away from what he actually said, plus a couple of smaller edits picked up along the way.

items.why: Carnegie said “a great business.” The leader version does not appear in his 1899 remarks or in the 1902 biography that reprinted them; the earliest “leader” printing in Quote Investigator’s chronology ↗ is a Deseret News item of 15 November 1975.

The 1899 newspaper text reads “all the credit of doing it.” The change to “for” was made by Barnard Alderson’s 1902 biography, which is where most later quoters picked it up — visible on pages 57–58 of the scanned edition ↗.
Both documented printings keep the second “to”: “or to get all the credit.” Quote Investigator ↗ records the clipped phrasing in a 2012 Longview, Texas newspaper column.
A 1992 motivational book, Building a POSitive Attitude, printed a de-gendered version, per Quote Investigator ↗. It circulates on business blogs alongside the leader form.

Neither wording appears in his Autobiography ↗, and the quotation is absent from Wikiquote’s Carnegie page ↗ in any form. It survives because a reporter wrote it down, not because Carnegie published it.

misattribution.truthLine: What he actually said, in an interview published 15 October 1899: “No man will make a great business who wants to do it all himself, or to get all the credit of doing it. That spirit is fatal, and the sure proof of a small mind.” The second sentence — the sharpest part — is almost never quoted. Quote Investigator ↗

context.heading: Why he said it about business, not leadership
lead: The line comes out of a specific boast. Asked in 1899 how young men get rich, Carnegie turned the question toward his partners — thirty-two of them, promoted out of his own works and given stock. “All are equal to each other, as the members of the Cabinet are equal,” he said. “The chief must only be first among equals.”

That is the setting for the famous sentence, and it explains the original noun. Carnegie was not offering a theory of leadership; he was explaining why a company outgrows any one owner, and why hoarding recognition is, in his words, “the sure proof of a small mind.” Two years later he sold Carnegie Steel to J. P. Morgan and the partners he had been describing were made rich alongside him.
detailsBody: The swap is easy to explain: the sentence reads as leadership advice, and by the 1970s that is how anthologists wanted to use it. Quote Investigator’s chronology shows the intermediate steps — the 1902 biography quietly changed “credit of doing it” to “credit for doing it,” a 1946 management book repeated the business version, and only in 1975 does “leader” appear, in a Deseret News notice for a volunteer center.

From there it hardened. Roy B. Zuck’s 1997 The Speaker’s Quote Book lists the “leader” form under Leadership, and by 2012 a Texas newspaper was printing it with the second “to” dropped as well — the exact shape most quote sites carry today.
context.pull: “The chief must only be first among equals.”

sourcesVerified.claim: Quote Investigator traces the quotation to an interview with Andrew Carnegie published 15 October 1899 in the St. Louis Globe-Democrat, with the original wording “No man will make a great business who wants to do it all himself, or to get all the credit of doing it. That spirit is fatal, and the sure proof of a small mind.” It also documents the same-day Philadelphia Times printing, the St. Paul Globe of 29 October 1899, the 1902 Alderson biography changing “of” to “for”, a 1946 Harvey Stowers book, the 1975 Deseret News “leader” substitution, a 1992 “person” version, the 1997 Speaker’s Quote Book “leader” entry, and a 2012 Longview, Texas printing dropping the second “to”. QI concludes Carnegie deserves credit for the 1899 statements and that altered versions later entered circulation.

The 1902 book Andrew Carnegie: The Man and His Work by Barnard Alderson contains, on pages 57–58, the passage “I do not believe any one man can make a success of a business nowadays. I am sure I never could have done so without my partners, of whom I had thirty-two… No man will make a great business who wants to do it all himself or to get all the credit for doing it. I believe firmly in youths as executive agents. Older heads should be reserved for counsel.”
The Internet Archive item is Andrew Carnegie; the man and his work by Alderson, published 1902 by Doubleday, Page & Co., New York, with full text available, and is recorded as not in copyright.

Andrew Carnegie was born 25 November 1835 and died 11 August 1919; he was a Scottish-American industrialist and philanthropist who emigrated to Allegheny, Pennsylvania in 1848 and sold Carnegie Steel Company to J. P. Morgan in 1901.

Wikiquote’s Andrew Carnegie page does not contain any quotation about making “a great business” or “a great leader” and getting “all the credit” in any of its sections, and gives his dates as 25 November 1835 – 11 August 1919.

Goodreads carries the altered wording “No man will make a great leader who wants to do it all himself or to get all the credit for doing it” attributed to Andrew Carnegie with no source book or date, and notes that quotes are added by the community and not verified.

Project Gutenberg ebook 17976 is the Autobiography of Andrew Carnegie (1835-1919); a full-text search of its plain-text edition returns no occurrence of the phrase “all the credit” or “great business”, confirming the quotation is not in his memoir.
